summary:
Apollo Life System is an offline health-monitoring companion for astronauts on long-duration missions, developed for the Brazilian Space Agency’s challenge at NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Astronauts can record vital signs and complete daily check-ins covering sleep, fatigue, mood, symptoms, hydration, and self-care, alongside tracking exercise, medications, and radiation exposure. Apollo compares measurements with each astronaut’s personal baseline and sourced medical ranges, then examines trends over time and combinations of indicators, not just isolated readings, to identify patterns that may signal concerns such as building stress, insufficient sleep, declining fitness, or possible infection. It presents these findings as understandable observations with evidence-backed next steps, not diagnoses.

Environment-specific measurement guidance, reminders, progress streaks, a spaceflight health library, and step-by-step emergency protocols help astronauts monitor their well-being and decide what action to take. A private onboard logbook stores records offline, while crew members control what is shared with medical support.

By bringing individual measurements together over time, Apollo helps astronauts recognize meaningful changes, understand what they may indicate, and respond even when immediate guidance from Earth is unavailable. The prototype uses simulated crew data calibrated against published spaceflight research and clinical references.
details:
Apollo Life System

Github link: https://github.com/PranavRodagi/apollo-life-system

Apollo Life System is a fully offline astronaut health-monitoring and analysis platform. We built it for the Brazilian Space Agency’s challenge at NASA Space Apps 2026. On a Mars mission the flight surgeon can be 22 minutes away one way, and sometimes out of contact for days. Apollo lets astronauts measure, understand and act on their own health data without waiting for Earth. It never diagnoses. It reports observations and what they “can be a sign of.”

What does it do, and how does it work?

Everything runs on the onboard computer: a local web app, a local analysis engine and a local database. Nothing needs a connection to Earth.

Personalized onboarding. Before launch, astronauts complete a nine-step setup stored privately onboard. They enter body measurements, health history (conditions, medications, allergies, supplements), a mission plan (phases, crew sleep schedule, EVA days) and their environment. Each condition can be linked to areas Apollo should watch more closely, such as sleep, fatigue, mood or weight. A flight surgeon can also set a care-plan range, which adds a matching reading and reminder. Crew members can opt in to menstrual-cycle tracking, or decide later, and it stays private unless they choose to share it. Only a family name is required, and every other step can be skipped and edited later.

The environment changes measurement instructions, emergency steps and the signal delay shown.

Daily monitoring. A 45-second daily check-in captures sleep, fatigue, mood, stress, symptoms, hydration and self-care. Guided four-step flows cover heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, breathing rate, blood glucose and weight. Each explains how to measure, why it matters in space and what to do if a reading needs attention. A wrist-actigraph card shows sleep, light exposure, activity and bedtime regularity.

Intelligent, multi-indicator analysis. Apollo goes beyond flagging out-of-range readings. It looks at measurements together and shows what they may mean together: for example, a small shift in sleep, fatigue, mood and stress can add up to a possible concern that no single reading would reveal. Four complementary methods run locally:

  • EWMA control charts learn each astronaut’s personal baseline and flag meaningful deviations from it.
  • Mann-Kendall tests with Theil-Sen slope show whether an indicator is rising, falling or stable.
  • Gradient-boosted classifiers recognize five patterns across indicators: insufficient sleep, building stress, declining fitness, inadequate oxygen and possible infection.
  • Isolation Forest flags unusual combinations of measurements.

Countermeasures and emergency mode. When a concern appears, Apollo offers sourced countermeasures and prevention guidance. Emergency mode is reachable offline from every screen. It gives one instruction at a time for collapse, chest pain, difficulty breathing, severe bleeding, fire, smoke or toxic air, and anything else. It includes branching questions, equipment guides, a CPR timer and metronome, and a timestamped action log. A radiation tracker compares dosimeter readings against NASA’s career limit and projects exposure through the mission.

Body & info: an offline health reference. A built-in library covers 12 spaceflight-related conditions, from space motion sickness and back pain to vision changes (SANS), bone loss and kidney stones. Astronauts can find them by body region or search. Each entry explains what the condition is, why it happens in space, what helps, when to call for help, which vitals relate to it and which NASA Human Research Program risk it belongs to. Prevention cards cover risks the app can’t measure onboard, such as immune changes, bone density, nutrition and mood, with everyday habits linked to sources. Vision-check reminders follow NASA’s operational schedule.

Exercise tracking. Astronauts log sessions by type (resistance, treadmill, cycle, bodyweight), minutes, device and effort. Apollo offers only the equipment actually available in the current environment, such as the compact exercise device in transit or ARED, T2 and CEVIS on a station. Weekly minutes are shown against the ISS reference of about two hours a day, which helps crews counter muscle and bone loss and feeds Apollo’s fitness analysis.

Private logbook. All records stay in an onboard logbook. At a communication window, only the categories the astronaut chose to share go to medical support.

What benefits does it have?

  • Works with no link to Earth. Guidance, analysis and emergency protocols never wait for a signal.
  • Personal, not just population. Every reading is compared with the astronaut’s own usual range and with medical limits, and both are shown, so small personal changes are caught early.
  • Fast to use. A 45-second check-in, guided measurements and one-instruction-at-a-time emergencies keep the crew’s workload low.
  • Trustworthy. 102 sources, NASA first. Every medical value is labelled verified, convention or app choice, and every countermeasure shows where it comes from.
  • Private by default. The astronaut decides what is shared with medical support, and when.

What is the intended impact?

Apollo is meant to give crews on long missions to the Moon and Mars a dependable way to look after their own health when help is minutes or days away. It turns readings into plain next steps, catches slow changes before they become problems, and gives the flight surgeon a clean, consented record when a link opens. The same approach could serve people in remote places on Earth, such as Antarctic stations, ships and isolated clinics.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Back end: FastAPI with a local SQLite database.
  • Analysis: NumPy and scikit-learn (EWMA control charts, Mann-Kendall with Theil-Sen, gradient-boosted classifiers, Isolation Forest).
  • Front end: React and Vite, in light and dark themes, on desktop and phone.
  • Testing: 267 automated tests with pytest.
  • Hardware supported in the design: the Canadian Space Agency’s Bio-Monitor shirt, the Brazilian Condor wrist actigraph (flown on Artemis II), and onboard medical kit devices. These are simulated in the prototype.
  • NASA and partner data: NASA-STD-3001 and OCHMO technical briefs, NASA Human Research Program risks, Curiosity RAD radiation measurements, ISS crew studies, and the NASA AMMOS Aerie mission-plan format.

How is our project creative?

  • It reads measures together, not one at a time, to show what they may mean together, while never claiming a diagnosis.
  • One overall graph puts different measures side by side by drawing each against the astronaut’s own usual range.
  • The app adapts to where the crew is: microgravity in transit, a space station, the lunar surface or a two-person rover.
  • It tracks radiation against NASA’s career limit and projects the rest of the mission from real Curiosity measurements.
  • The streak rewards complete days, not good numbers, so honest entries on bad days still count.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Safety: the app never diagnoses or suggests medication, and points to emergency mode and the flight surgeon whenever a reading needs attention.
  • Evidence: every medical value comes from NASA first, then accepted clinical standards; values without a source were removed.
  • Honesty about data: no open daily astronaut health dataset exists, so the models were trained and tested on simulated crews tuned to published ISS figures, and the app says so.
  • Privacy: mood, symptoms and notes stay private unless the astronaut chooses to share them.
  • Accessibility: large text, and colour always paired with a word.
  • Crew workload and environment: short check-ins, quiet hours during sleep, and instructions that change with gravity and distance from Earth.
